description: Hands-on NoSQL challenges and flashcards covering MongoDB (document store), Redis (key-value), Cassandra (wide-column), and core NoSQL concepts for the CodeConfidence NoSQL Shell section.

questions.title: Insert Documents into MongoDB
questions.prompt: Insert a collection called 'students'. Add 3 student documents with fields: name, age, department, gpa, skills (array), address (nested object with city and pincode).
questions.solution:
// Switch to database
use codeConfidenceDB

// Insert multiple documents
db.students.insertMany([
  {
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 20,
    department: 'CS',
    gpa: 9.1,
    skills: ['Python', 'SQL', 'Machine Learning'],
    address: { city: 'Bangalore', pincode: '560001' },
    enrolled_on: new Date('2022-08-01')
  },
  {
    name: 'Bob',
    age: 21,
    department: 'IT',
    gpa: 8.3,
    skills: ['Java', 'Spring Boot', 'Docker'],
    address: { city: 'Mysore', pincode: '570001' },
    enrolled_on: new Date('2022-08-01')
  },
  {
    name: 'Carol',
    age: 20,
    department: 'CS',
    gpa: 9.5,
    skills: ['JavaScript', 'React', 'Node.js', 'MongoDB'],
    address: { city: 'Bangalore', pincode: '560002' },
    enrolled_on: new Date('2022-08-01')
  }
])

questions.title: MongoDB Query with Filters
questions.prompt: Write MongoDB queries to: (1) Find all CS students with GPA > 9.0, (2) Find students who know 'Python', (3) Find students from Bangalore sorted by GPA descending, (4) Find students with exactly 3 skills.
ai_review_hints: Use dot notation ('address.city') to query nested fields.
MongoDB automatically checks if an array contains a value — no special operator needed for simple array contains.

questions.title: MongoDB Update Operations
questions.prompt: Write queries to: (1) Update Alice's GPA to 9.5, (2) Add 'TensorFlow' to Alice's skills array, (3) Remove 'Docker' from Bob's skills, (4) Increment all CS students' GPA by 0.1 (max 10).

questions.title: MongoDB Aggregation Pipeline
questions.prompt: Write an aggregation pipeline to: show each department, count of students, average GPA, and list of all student names — filtered to departments with avg GPA above 8.5, sorted by avg GPA descending.
ai_review_hints: Aggregation pipeline stages execute in order — each stage feeds into the next.
$match after $group filters groups (like SQL HAVING). $match before $group filters documents (like SQL WHERE).
Use $push to accumulate values into an array in $group.

questions.title: MongoDB Indexes
questions.prompt: Create: (1) a single-field index on department, (2) a compound index on department + gpa (desc), (3) a text index on name for text search. Then query using the text index.

questions.title: Redis Basic Commands
questions.prompt: Write Redis commands to: (1) Set a key 'student:1:name' to 'Alice' with expiry of 1 hour, (2) Get the value, (3) Check TTL, (4) Increment a counter 'visits:homepage', (5) Check if a key exists.
questions.solution:
# 1. SET with expiry (EX = seconds)
SET student:1:name "Alice" EX 3600

# Or with SETEX
SETEX student:1:name 3600 "Alice"

# 2. GET value
GET student:1:name
# → "Alice"

# 3. Check TTL (returns seconds remaining, -1 = no expiry, -2 = key gone)
TTL student:1:name

# 4. Increment counter (atomic)
INCR visits:homepage
# → 1
INCR visits:homepage
# → 2
INCRBY visits:homepage 5
# → 7

# 5. Check if key exists
EXISTS student:1:name
# → 1 (exists) or 0 (not found)

# Delete a key
DEL student:1:name

questions.title: Redis Hash – Store Structured Data
questions.prompt: Use Redis Hashes to store a student object (id, name, department, gpa). Then update gpa, retrieve a single field, and get all fields.
questions.solution:
# Store student as hash
HMSET student:1001 name "Alice" department "CS" gpa "9.1" age "20"

# Or one field at a time
HSET student:1001 email "alice@college.edu"

# Get one field
HGET student:1001 name
# → "Alice"

# Get multiple fields
HMGET student:1001 name gpa department

# Get all fields and values
HGETALL student:1001

# Update a field
HSET student:1001 gpa "9.5"

# Increment numeric field
HINCRBYFLOAT student:1001 gpa 0.2

# Delete a field from hash
HDEL student:1001 age

# Check if field exists in hash
HEXISTS student:1001 email

# Count fields in hash
HLEN student:1001

questions.title: Redis Lists & Sets – Leaderboard & Unique Tags
questions.prompt: (1) Use a Redis List to implement a recent activity log (max 5 items). (2) Use a Sorted Set (ZSET) to build a leaderboard of students by score.
questions.solution:
# --- LISTS for Recent Activity Log ---
# Push to front of list
LPUSH activity:user1 "Solved DSA problem"
LPUSH activity:user1 "Read DBMS chapter"
LPUSH activity:user1 "Attempted mock test"

# Keep only last 5 items (trim list)
LTRIM activity:user1 0 4

# Get all items in list
LRANGE activity:user1 0 -1
# → ["Attempted mock test", "Read DBMS chapter", "Solved DSA problem"]

# Length of list
LLEN activity:user1

# --- SORTED SETS for Leaderboard ---
# Add members with scores
ZADD leaderboard 920 "Alice"
ZADD leaderboard 870 "Bob"
ZADD leaderboard 950 "Carol"
ZADD leaderboard 810 "Dave"

# Get top 3 students (highest score first)
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 2 WITHSCORES
# → ["Carol", 950, "Alice", 920, "Bob", 870]

# Get rank of a student (0-indexed, 0 = highest)
ZREVRANK leaderboard "Alice"
# → 1 (second place)

# Get Alice's score
ZSCORE leaderboard "Alice"
# → 920

# Update score
ZINCRBY leaderboard 30 "Bob"  # Bob now has 900

# Count students with score between 800 and 950
ZCOUNT leaderboard 800 950

questions.front: When should you use Redis vs a relational database?
questions.back: Use Redis for: session storage, caching (reduce DB load), rate limiting, leaderboards, pub/sub messaging, real-time counters, job queues. Use RDBMS for: persistent structured data, complex relationships, ACID transactions, reporting.

CAP theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee at most 2 of 3 properties:
• Consistency (C): All nodes see the same data at the same time
• Availability (A): Every request gets a response (may be stale)
• Partition Tolerance (P): System works even when network partitions occur

Examples:
• CP systems: MongoDB, HBase, Zookeeper (consistent + partition tolerant)
• AP systems: Cassandra, CouchDB, DynamoDB (available + partition tolerant)
• CA systems: Traditional RDBMS (not partition tolerant — single node)

Eventual consistency means that if no new updates are made to a piece of data, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value — but at any given moment, different nodes may return different values. This is favored by AP systems (like DynamoDB, Cassandra) for high availability at the cost of immediate consistency.
questions.example: Amazon shopping cart: You add an item on your phone. For a few seconds, your laptop might not show it yet. Eventually both devices sync.

questions.front: What are the 4 types of NoSQL databases and when to use each?
questions.back:
1. Document Store (MongoDB, CouchDB): JSON-like documents. Use for: catalogs, user profiles, content management
2. Key-Value Store (Redis, DynamoDB): Simple key → value. Use for: caching, sessions, leaderboards, rate limiting
3. Wide-Column Store (Cassandra, HBase): Rows with dynamic columns. Use for: IoT data, time-series, analytics at massive scale
4. Graph Database (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune): Nodes and edges. Use for: social networks, recommendation engines, fraud detection
